s: Part two.
Few-shot examples.
By the end of this part, you'll know three things.
Why a model that understands the task still gives different answers on different runs.
Which examples actually fix that.
And the three ways people waste their examples.
Let's start with a picture.
Imagine a new football referee.
One week, a certain kind of tackle gets a yellow card.
The next week, the same tackle gets a red.
Now, what helps?
Reading them the rulebook again?
No.
They already know the rulebook.
What helps is this.
You find the tackles they keep flipping on.
You show them two clips of exactly those tackles.
And you explain the call on each one.
That's the whole idea of this part.
So here's the problem in plain terms.
Inconsistency is not the same as being wrong.
The model understands the task.
It just lands on a genuinely unclear boundary differently from one run to the next.
And the fix is to show, not tell.
The technical name for showing is few-shot prompting.
You put a small number of worked examples in the prompt.
The course is clear on one thing.
Examples are the most dependable lever you have on format, tone, and structure.
But here's the part that surprises people.
Their value for accuracy depends entirely on which cases you pick.
The instinct is to pick clean, tidy, typical examples.
That instinct is backwards.
An easy example teaches the model nothing it wasn't already doing right.
The accuracy lives in the cases where your own rules are unclear.
Why can't you just write better rules?
The course has a name for this.
The instruction ceiling.
Words like "severe" or "significant" get read through the model's general training, not through your team's meaning.
So another paragraph of definitions doesn't remove the ambiguity.
It just moves it somewhere else.
Hold on to this line.
Instructions describe.
Examples demonstrate.
How many examples?
Honestly, the sources disagree.
The lesson fifteen deck says two to four.
The study notes, following Anthropic's guidance, say three to five.
So don't hang an answer on the count.
What both agree on is this.
A small set, aimed at the unclear cases, beats a big set aimed at coverage.
Exam tip.
If an option says "nine examples, one per label," or "add six more," the size of the number is your clue.
That's the wrong answer.
Now the design rules.
There are seven, so I'll take them one at a time.
One.
Pick the cases people actually argued about.
Two.
Put a near miss on each side of the line.
Three.
Balance the outcomes, so the set doesn't quietly teach "the answer is usually yes."
Four.
Keep incidental details, like length, the same across labels.
Five.
Show the reasoning, not just the answer.
Six.
Where two labels are both defensible, write your house rule into the reasoning.
And seven.
Show the "I'm not sure" path at least once.
If you never show it, it never gets used.
In exam terms, three details.
First.
Each example goes in example tags, inside an examples block.
The tags tell the model which part is a demonstration, which part is an instruction, and which part is the real input.
Second.
Each example runs input, then reasoning, then output.
Why the reasoning?
Because output-only examples invite pattern matching.
The model asks, "which example does this look like?" instead of, "what's the rule?"
Show the working, and it learns a rule that carries over to layouts it has never seen.
And third, a limit to remember.
Examples make the right format likely.
They never make the wrong format impossible.
For a guarantee, you need the enforcement coming up in part three.
Quick recap before the questions.
Inconsistency means an unclear boundary, not a confused model.
Spend your few examples on that boundary.
Balance the outcomes.
Show the reasoning.
Right.
Four practice questions.
Question one.
Here's the scenario.
A review step labels bugs as critical, high, or medium.
The same kind of bug, a missing null check on an internal response, comes back critical on some runs and high on others.
The prompt already has about eight hundred words of severity definitions.
There's room for only a handful of examples.
What should the architect do first?
Take a second.
The answer.
Rerun a sample of the changes several times.
Find exactly where the severity flips.
Then add reasoning examples for those cases only.
In other words: diagnose the drift, then spend your examples on the fault line.
What would a good example say?
Something like this.
"The caller is internal.
The input is already checked upstream.
The failure is an error page, not a data leak.
So: high."
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: one tidy example per severity level, like SQL injection as critical.
Why is that wrong?
Because SQL injection is already stable.
You'd spend your budget on solid ground and leave the drifting case alone.
Wrong: sharper wording that separates "severe" from "significant."
Why?
That's the instruction ceiling again.
More words, same ambiguity.
Wrong: set the temperature to zero.
Why?
It freezes one of the two answers.
It doesn't decide which one is right.
Question two.
Here's the scenario.
A refund agent has four examples.
All four come from the most common kind of ticket.
And all four end with "approve refund."
In production, it approves forty-one percent of requests.
A policy review says only about fifteen percent should qualify.
And the reviewers agree the policy text itself is fine.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Replace the set with disputed cases, balanced between approve and deny, and include one that routes to human review.
A good set sounds like this.
An unopened item, inside the window.
Approve.
An opened item, with no defect.
Deny.
And that's a near miss, because opened items only qualify if they're faulty.
A defect reported just after the window.
Approve, under a house rule that defects count from the report date.
And a vague message, with no order identified.
That one is needs_human_review.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: add four more approval examples from other ticket types.
Why?
That widens coverage, but it deepens the lean.
Eight approvals just say "approve" louder.
Wrong: add a line saying "approve less often."
Why?
It doesn't say which requests qualify.
You'd trade wrong approvals for wrong denials.
Wrong: move the examples after the customer's message.
Why?
That changes where they sit, not what they teach.
Hold on to this line.
All-yes examples teach a lean, not a line.
Question three.
Here's the scenario.
A contract extractor has examples that show only an input contract and the output data.
Every example comes from a contract laid out as a table.
On contracts written as dense prose, it fills renewal_term with values it infers from other clauses.
There's room for two or three examples.
What's the fix?
Take a second.
The answer.
Rewrite the examples to show the reasoning.
Stated versus inferred, and why inferred means null.
And use both layouts, tables and prose.
A good example quotes a clause saying the agreement "continues until terminated."
It notes that twelve months only appears in the payment clause.
And so it returns null for renewal_term.
Here's a way to picture it.
Show a trainee three finished tax forms, and they learn what a finished form looks like.
Show them where each number came from on the receipt, and which boxes to leave blank when the receipt is silent, and they can fill in a form they've never seen.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: add six more output-only examples from table contracts.
Why?
It blows the budget and deepens the pattern matching.
Wrong: add a pattern check on the field's format.
Why?
A guessed duration is perfectly well formed.
The format was never the problem.
Wrong: "do not guess values," in capital letters.
Why?
It still doesn't say what counts as stated.
Question four.
This one is choose two.
Here's the scenario.
A ticket classifier sorts tickets into bug, feature request, and tech debt.
Accuracy is eighty-eight percent.
Nearly all the errors fall on two boundaries, where the engineers themselves argued until someone wrote down a house rule.
Which two properties should the example set have?
Take a second.
The answers.
First, examples drawn from those disputed boundary cases, with the house rule written into each example's reasoning.
Second, outcomes balanced across the labels, with incidental features, like ticket length, matched.
Here's the picture.
Teaching a child the difference between a wolf and a husky, you don't show them a poodle and a lion.
You show the husky that looks most like a wolf, and the wolf that looks most like a husky.
And one more thing.
Make sure the wolf photos aren't all taken in snow.
Otherwise the child learns that snow means wolf.
That's the surface-feature trap.
If every tech debt example is long, and every bug example is short, you've built a length detector.
Now the wrong turns.
Wrong: one example per label, from the busiest ticket types.
Why?
Volume isn't difficulty.
Wrong: examples the model already gets right.
Why?
Easy cases carry no boundary information.
Wrong: paste the examples in without tags, to save space.
Why?
The tags are what separate a demonstration from an instruction.
Two contrasts to lock this in.
First.
Rules versus examples.
When do you write a rule, and when do you show a case?
Write the rule first, like in part one, because a stated test can be checked.
Then use examples for whatever the rule still leaves unclear at the edges.
So on the exam: if the model understands the task but flips on the same kind of case, that's an examples problem.
If it's flagging far too much, that's a rules problem.
Second.
Examples versus a schema.
Examples make a format likely.
A schema makes anything else impossible.
If a question demands a guarantee, more examples are never the answer.
And the words in a question that should switch this part on.
"Inconsistent across runs."
That means targeted examples at the fault line.
"Room for only a handful."
That means spend them on boundaries, not coverage.
"The policy text is correct."
That means the problem is what's in the example set.
"A different document layout."
That means show the reasoning, not just the output.
That's part two.
If you remember one thing, make it this.
Spend your few examples on the cases people argue about.
Balance the outcomes.
And show the reasoning.
Coming up in part three: how to make the format not just likely, but guaranteed.
